cues.text: Imagine two people meet at a Japanese office in the morning.
Later, they meet again in the evening.
They do not just say the same "hello" both times.
A Japanese greeting changes with the time of day and with the people.
In Japan, bowing is the common greeting.
But not every bow is the same.
The bow changes with social status, so it depends on who is greeting whom.
A bow to a senior manager is not the same as a bow to a friend.
The words change too.
People say "konnichiwa" in the daytime and "konbanwa" in the evening.
They use these words when they meet someone for the first time that day.
So a Japanese greeting does more than say "I see you."
It also shows the time of day and how the two people are connected.
You can think of it like the address on a letter.
It is short, but it tells you where the letter is going.
In the same way, a short bow tells both people something about their relationship.
For a visitor, this has a practical side.
You do not need a perfect bow.
But it helps to notice that greetings in Japan follow the situation.
They are not one fixed action.
Now imagine a Japanese colleague invites you to their home.
This is a bigger moment than it may seem.
Being invited to a Japanese home is an honour.
Many Japanese people feel their homes are humble, which means simple or not special enough for guests.
So when someone opens their home to you, they are giving you something important.
Inside the home, you will find clear borders, and each border has its own rule.
At the entrance, people take off their shoes.
Then they put on indoor slippers.
When they step onto tatami, the straw mats on some floors, they take off the slippers too.
The bathroom is another border.
People take off their slippers there, and sometimes they put on special bathroom slippers instead.
So one short walk through a house can mean more than one change of footwear.
The rule is not just "no shoes inside."
The rule is that different parts of the home have different steps.
The entrance, the main rooms, the tatami room and the bathroom each have their own.
Think of it like the doors at an airport.
You pass one gate and follow one rule.
Then you pass the next gate and follow another.
A guest who follows these steps shows that they understand the home and respect the invitation.
At a Japanese meal, the table is a shared space.
Many rules exist to keep that space fair for everyone.
Before eating, people say "itadakimasu," a word of thanks at the start of the meal.
They also wait until everyone is ready before they start eating.
Nobody runs ahead of the group.
Shared dishes are common.
Everyone takes food from the same plates, so small actions matter.
If one piece of food is left, it is polite to ask before you take the last bite.
Leaving food on your own plate is seen as rude.
Together, these rules work like the rules of a team game.
Each person plays their part, so the whole table has a good meal.
Some rules are more flexible than visitors expect.
Sushi, for example, can be eaten with chopsticks or with your hands.
So the point is not to make every action strict.
The point is to respect the food and the other people at the table.
France shows a different place where manners begin.
In a French restaurant, the rules start at the door, before any food arrives.
Staff usually give guests a table.
Customers wait at the entrance until someone takes them to a table.
If you want a different table, you can ask, but you should ask politely.
In Japan, the clearest rules are around sharing the food.
In France, an important rule comes at the start: let the staff guide you.
Here is a question many visitors ask: if you do not tip, why would the service be good?
In Japan, tipping is generally not practised.
Sometimes a service charge is already part of the price.
But Japanese service is known for being very polite and careful.
So the missing tip does not mean missing effort.
The reason lies in an idea about customers.
In Japan, the customer is treated almost like a god.
Good service is part of the job and part of the price, not an extra that you pay for at the end.
If you leave money on the table, it can seem strange, because the work was already expected.
Paying has its own manners too.
It is proper to put your money on a small tray, not to hand it straight to the person.
Like the slippers at a doorway, the tray is a small step that shows care.
So the link between money and service is different here.
In some places, a tip is a way to say "thank you for good service."
In Japan, the thank-you is already part of the system, and the service is the starting point.
All these customs share one habit: careful attention to small steps.
You can see the same habit in Japan's fast trains.
The Tokaido Shinkansen is a high-speed line in Japan.
In 2024, it ran 383 trains a day and carried about 460,000 passengers.
Those trains had an average delay of just 1.4 minutes per train.
That is about 84 seconds.
Now think about the size of the job.
If 460,000 people share 383 trains, that is about 1,200 people per train on average.
Each person must get on and off quickly, every train must leave on time, and this happens all day.
This is where the small habits matter.
A delay on one train can spread to the next one, like a line of people at a shop.
When one person stops, everyone behind them waits too.
So a short average delay is not only about fast machines.
It also depends on many small, careful actions, repeated hundreds of times a day.
Bowing to the right person, changing slippers at the right door and leaving a train exactly on time may seem very different.
But they all show the same thing: people paying close attention to the small step in front of them.
